headline: White House worker bet on Trump's words

sources.title: Officials probe whether White House teleprompter operator profited off Trump's words
Trump suspends teleprompter operator over Kalshi bets allegations, White House says
White House teleprompter operator investigated over alleged Kalshi trades on Trump speeches
White House teleprompter operator being investigated after alleged bets on Trump speeches (video, NBC News)

chunks.text: [[Regulators]] in the United States are {{digging into}} a White House worker who ran the president's [[teleprompter]]. His job was to load the words that President Trump reads during his [[speeches]]. [[Because of this]], the worker could {{find out}} [[exactly]] what the president would say before anyone else. Officials say he used this [[early access]] to [[bet money]], and the bets {{panned out}}, [[earning]] him almost $100,000.

verbs.correct: To search deeply for the facts about a topic
verbs.wrong: To officially punish a person for wrongdoing
verbs.why: Reporters dig into a scandal, and detectives dig into old case files for new clues. Regulators are digging into a White House worker who ran the president's teleprompter.

verbs.correct: To learn a fact that you did not know before
verbs.wrong: To solve a hard problem by thinking carefully
verbs.why: Detectives find out the truth through evidence, and reporters find out secrets through sources. Because of his job, the worker could find out the president's exact words before anyone else.

verbs.wrong: To become known to the public
verbs.why: A risky investment can pan out well, and a new business plan can pan out after a slow start. The worker's bets on the president's exact words panned out, earning him almost $100,000.

chunks.text: The bets were placed on a [[prediction]] website called Kalshi. On the site, users try to [[predict]] which exact words a speaker will use. Because the worker had already {{gone through}} the president's scripts, he could easily {{cash in on}} what he knew. This gave him an [[unfair]] [[advantage]] over other users, who were only [[guessing]].

verbs.correct: To read or examine something carefully in full
verbs.wrong: To photocopy every single page for filing
verbs.why: Lawyers go through contracts line by line, and pilots go through a safety checklist before takeoff. The worker had already gone through the president's scripts before placing his bets.

verbs.correct: To use a situation to make money or profit
verbs.wrong: To exchange something like a ticket for money
verbs.why: Companies cash in on a popular trend, and investors cash in on rising prices. The worker cashed in on his early access to the president's speeches to place winning bets.

chunks.text: The [[scheme]] did not stay secret [[for long]]. Kalshi's security team {{picked up on}} the [[strange]] [[betting]] pattern and {{handed over}} the case to a government agency, the CFTC. The company also {{closed down}} his account and kept about $90,000 of his [[winnings]].

verbs.correct: To notice something that is not obvious
verbs.wrong: To learn a new skill slowly through practice
verbs.why: A good teacher picks up on a student's mistake, and a nurse picks up on small changes in a patient. Kalshi's security team picked up on a strange pattern in the worker's betting.

verbs.correct: To give something or someone to another person
verbs.wrong: To photograph the entire case file quickly
verbs.why: Police hand over evidence to prosecutors, and a company can hand over a case to federal investigators. Kalshi handed the case over to the CFTC once the strange pattern was noticed.

verbs.correct: To stop a business or service from operating
verbs.wrong: To briefly pause something and start it again
verbs.why: Banks close down suspicious accounts, and cities sometimes close down a business for breaking the rules. Kalshi closed down the worker's account and kept about $90,000 of his winnings.

chunks.text: [[For now]], the worker has been {{put on}} [[unpaid leave]] while the [[investigation]] {{keeps on}} running. Officials want to know whether he [[broke any rules]] by using private information. [[In the end]], the CFTC may make him {{give back}} most of the money he won.

verbs.correct: To place someone into a certain status or condition
verbs.wrong: To give someone an extra job or duty to do
verbs.why: A company can put a worker on probation, and a school can put a student on a warning. The White House put the teleprompter operator on unpaid leave during the investigation.

verbs.correct: To continue doing something without stopping
verbs.wrong: To start something again after it has stopped
verbs.why: Rain can keep on falling all day, and a heated debate can keep on going for hours. The investigation into the worker keeps on running while officials try to learn more.

verbs.correct: To return something to the person it belongs to
verbs.wrong: To publicly sign a written apology letter
verbs.why: Borrowers give back loans with interest, and thieves are sometimes ordered to give back stolen money. The CFTC may eventually make the worker give back most of what he won.

mainIdea.s: Regulators are digging into a White House worker who used early access to speeches to win almost 100,000 dollars. A security team on the betting site caught the pattern and reported the case.
mainIdea.why: The story says the worker used early access to the speech to win almost 100,000 dollars. Kalshi's security team caught the strange pattern and reported the case.

mainIdea.s: A federal agency first noticed the strange betting, and that report led Kalshi to look into the worker on its own. The worker has already paid back every dollar he won from the bets.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Kalshi's own security team noticed the strange betting first, not a federal agency. The article also says the CFTC may make him give back the money later, not that he already paid it all back.

mainIdea.s: A separate review is checking whether other government workers used inside information to trade stocks for profit. That review covers several departments and began for unrelated reasons.
mainIdea.why: This is about a different review of government workers trading stocks, not the teleprompter case. The real story is about one worker betting on the president's exact words.

tf.s: Kalshi closed down its whole website after the scandal.
tf.why: Kalshi closed down only the worker's account, not the entire website.

tf.s: Regulators are digging into the worker who ran the president's teleprompter.
tf.why: The story says regulators are digging into the White House worker who operated the teleprompter.

tf.s: Kalshi's security team picked up on the strange betting pattern.
tf.why: Kalshi's security noticed the unusual pattern and reported the case to the CFTC.

tf.s: The worker could only find out the speech words after the president had spoken them.
tf.why: He could find out the words before the president spoke, which gave him an unfair advantage.

tf.s: The worker has been put on unpaid leave during the investigation.
tf.why: The story says the worker was put on unpaid leave while officials investigate.

tf.s: The worker gave back the money on his own before anyone noticed.
tf.why: He did not give back the money himself; Kalshi froze his winnings and the CFTC may make him give back most of it.
